```{r echo = F}
y_1 <- df(x, df1 = 2, df2 = 100)
y_2 <- df(x, df1 = 4, df2 = 400)

f_plot <- data.table(x = x, "F(2,100)" = y_1, "F(4,400)" = y_2) %>%
  melt(id.var = "x")

ggplot(data = f_plot) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x, y = value, color = variable)) +
  scale_color_discrete(name = "") +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```
:::
<!--end of the 1st column-->
::: {.column width="40%"}
**F-test steps**

+ Define the null hypothesis
+ Estimate the unrestricted and restricted models to obtains their $SSR$
+ Calculate $F$-statistic
+ Define the significance level and corresponding critical value according to the F distribution with appropriate degrees of freedoms
+ Reject if your $F$-statistic is greater than the critical value, otherwise do not reject
:::
<!--end of the 2nd column-->
:::
<!--end of the columns-->

### F-test by hand

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Step 1 

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Step one in code: fit both models. The unrestricted one has all five regressors; the restricted one drops exactly the three the null sets to zero. Then compute each sum of squared residuals by squaring the residuals and adding them up. Read the two model formulas side by side and check that the only difference is those three variables. That is what makes the comparison valid: everything else about the two fits, the data, the other regressors, the estimator, is identical.

</details>

Estimate the unrestricted and restricted models

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
#--- unrestricted model ---#
reg_u <- feols(log(salary) ~ years + gamesyr +
  bavg + hrunsyr + rbisyr, data = mlb1)

SSR_u <- sum(reg_u$residuals^2)

#--- restricted model ---#
reg_r <- feols(log(salary) ~ years + gamesyr, data = mlb1)

SSR_r <- sum(reg_r$residuals^2)
```

#### Step 2

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Now assemble the statistic. Three restrictions, so `df_q` is three. The residual degrees of freedom come from the unrestricted fit. Then the numerator is the gap divided by the number of restrictions, and the denominator is the unrestricted sum of squared residuals divided by its degrees of freedom. Notice what that denominator is: it is essentially sigma-hat squared, the estimated error variance. So the F-statistic is comparing the fit you gained against the noise level, which is the natural way to make a gap unit-free.

</details>

Calculate F-stat

```{webr-r}
df_q <- 3 # the number of restrictions
df_ur <- degrees_freedom(reg_u, "resid") # degrees of freedom for the unrestricted model
F_stat_num <- (SSR_r - SSR_u) / df_q # numerator of F-stat
F_stat_denom <- SSR_u / df_ur # denominator of F-stat
F_sta <- F_stat_num / F_stat_denom # F-stat
F_sta
```

#### Steps 3 and 4

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

The critical value comes from `qf`, and note it needs both degrees of freedom arguments. Five percent significance, so we want the ninety-fifth percentile, and because the test is one-tailed by construction there is no halving. Run the comparison. It comes back true, and read the callout: the three performance variables *are* jointly significant, even though not one of them was individually significant at ten percent. That is a genuine contradiction of the naive reading, and the question at the bottom is the right one to ask.

</details>

Find the critical value

```{webr-r}
alpha <- 0.05 # 5%  significance level
c_value <- qf(1 - alpha, df1 = df_q, df2 = df_ur)
c_value
```

Is F-stat > critical value?

```{webr-r}
F_sta > c_value
```

:::{.callout-note title="Observation"}
So, the performance variables have statistically significant impacts on salary <span style = "color: red;"> jointly</span>!!

What happened?
:::

:::
<!--end of panel-->

### F-test (easier way)

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### How

<details class="transcript inline">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

The practical version. `car::linearHypothesis` takes the unrestricted fit and the restrictions written as text, and does everything we just did by hand. Read the note about the hypothesis argument: it is a character vector, one string per restriction, and each string is an equation. You are not limited to testing against zero, which is worth knowing; you can test whether a coefficient equals one, or whether two coefficients are equal, using exactly the same function.

</details>

You can use the `car::linearHypothesis()` function from the `car` package. 

<br>

**Syntax**

```{r eval = F}
car::linearHypothesis(regression, hypothesis)
```

+ `regression`: the name of the regression results of the unrestricted model

+ `hypothesis`: text of the null hypothesis. For example,

`c("x1 = 0", "x2 = 1")` means the coefficients on $x1$ and $x2$ are $0$ and $1$, respectively

#### Demonstration

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

And here it is on the baseball model. Three restrictions in one vector, all setting a coefficient to zero. Run it and compare the statistic against the one you computed by hand two tabs ago. They should match. From now on this is what you will use, but I wanted you to build it once from sums of squared residuals so that the number means something. If you ever get a surprising F-test result, knowing it is a comparison of two model fits is what lets you work out why.

</details>

The following code test if $\beta_{bavg} = 0$, $\beta_{hrunsyr} = 0$, and $\beta_{rbisyr} = 0$. 

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
#--- F-test ---#
car::linearHypothesis(mlb_reg, c("bavg=0", "hrunsyr=0", "rbisyr=0"))
```

:::
<!--end of panel-->

:::
<!--end of panel-->

## Simulation (multicollinearity, t-test, and F-test)


::: {.panel-tabset}

### Data generation

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

A simulation to pin down what just happened, and the construction should look familiar. `x1` and `x2` are each built mostly from a shared term `mu`, so they are strongly correlated by design. `x3` is independent. And read the line that builds y: all three variables have a coefficient of one, so all three genuinely matter, and we know that because we chose it. Run the correlation cell and see how close to one it is. This is the same data generating process as Case two in the multicollinearity lecture.

</details>

```{webr-r}
N <- 300 # num observations
mu <- runif(N) # term shared by indep vars 1 and 2
x1 <- 0.1 * runif(N) + 2 * mu # indep 1
x2 <- 0.1 * runif(N) + 2 * mu # indep 2
x3 <- runif(N) # indep 3
u <- rnorm(N) # error
y <- 1 + x1 + x2 + x3 + u # generate y
data <- data.table(y = y, x1 = x1, x2 = x2, x3 = x3) # combine into a data.table
```

<br>

`x1` and `x2` are highly correlated with each other:

```{webr-r}
cor(x1, x2) # correlation between x1 and x2
```


### Regression

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Run the regression and look at the two rows for `x1` and `x2`. Both are insignificant, and we know for certain that both have a true coefficient of one, because we wrote it. So this is a case where the individual t-tests are unambiguously giving you the wrong impression, and unlike with the baseball data there is no arguing about it. Look at the standard errors specifically rather than the estimates. They are enormous, and that is the mechanism: not wrong estimates, but imprecise ones.

</details>

```{webr-r}
reg_u <- fixest::feols(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = data) # OLS
broom::tidy(reg_u) # results
```

<br>

Both `x1` and `x2` are statistically insignificant individually. 

### F-test

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Now the joint test, built by hand so you can see it is the same machinery. The restricted model drops both correlated variables and keeps only `x3`, so there are two restrictions. Compute both sums of squared residuals, form the ratio, and compare against the critical value from `qf`. Run it and look at the size of the F-statistic. It is not marginal; it is enormous. The two variables that individually looked like noise are, taken together, overwhelmingly important, which is exactly what we built into the data.

</details>

```{webr-r}
#--- unrestricted ---#
SSR_u <- sum(reg_u$residuals^2)

#--- restricted ---#
reg_r <- fixest::feols(y ~ x3, data = data)
SSR_r <- sum(reg_r$residuals^2)

#--- degrees of freedom of residuals ---#
df_resid <- degrees_freedom(reg_u, "resid")

#--- F ---#
F_stat <- ((SSR_r - SSR_u) / 2) / (SSR_u / df_resid)

#--- critical value ---#
alpha <- 0.05
(
  c_value <- qf(1 - alpha, df1 = 2, df2 = df_resid)
)
```

<br>

The F-statistic for the hypothesis testing is:

```{webr-r}
#--- F > critical value? ---#
F_stat
F_stat > c_value
```

<br>

The F-statistic is very high, meaning they collectively affect the dependent variable significantly.


### Important

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

The explanation, and then the connection back. The standard errors are large because the two variables are so alike that the estimation cannot tell their individual contributions apart. Read the callout, because this is lecture 04 seen from the other side. There we showed correlation inflates the variance through the one minus R-squared-j term. A bigger variance means a bigger standard error, and a bigger standard error means a smaller t-statistic. The insignificance you saw is that inflation, arriving at the testing stage. The F-test dodges it by never asking about the variables one at a time.

</details>

The standard error estimates of the coefficients on `x1` and `x2` are very high because they are so highly correlated that the estimation had a hard time distinguishing their individual impacts.

But collectively they have large impacts, and the $F$-test was able to detect the statistical significance of their impacts <span style = "color: red;"> collectively</span>.

<br>

:::{.callout-important title="This is lecture 04, seen from the other side"}
The data generating process here is Case 2 from the multicollinearity lecture: two regressors sharing a common term. There we showed that correlation inflates $Var(\widehat{\beta}_j)$ through the $1-R^2_j$ term in the denominator.

A large variance means a large standard error, and a large standard error means a <span style = "color: red;"> small </span> t-statistic &mdash; which is exactly the insignificance you see on the `Regression` tab. Multicollinearity did not make the estimates wrong; it made them too imprecise to distinguish individually. The $F$-test sidesteps the problem entirely by never asking about them one at a time.
:::

:::
<!--end of panel-->

## MLB example

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Correlation check

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Back to the baseball data, to check whether the same mechanism explains what we saw there. Run the correlation matrix on the three performance variables. Home runs per year and runs batted in per year are strongly correlated, which makes sense: a home run drives in at least one run by definition, so a player who hits many home runs mechanically has a high runs-batted-in figure. Batting average is much less related to either. So two of the three are near-duplicates, and that is enough to produce what we saw.

</details>

Here is the correlation coefficients between the three variables:

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
dplyr::select(mlb1, bavg, hrunsyr, rbisyr) %>% cor()
```

As you can see, `rbisyr` and `hrunsyr` are highly correlated with each other. 

They are not so highly correlated with `bavg`.



### Multiple coefficients again

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

One last connection, and it ties the two halves of this lecture together. Testing a linear combination is just an F-test with one restriction. The fact underneath is exact: F with one numerator degree of freedom is the square of t on the same denominator degrees of freedom. Run the cell, which takes the square root of the chi-squared value, and compare against the t-statistic we computed by hand on the college slide. Same number. So there were never two procedures here, only one written two ways.

</details>

The test of a linear combination of the parameters we looked at earlier is a special case of F-test where the number of restriction is 1. 

It can be shown that square root of $F_{1, df}$ follows the $t_{df}$ distribution.

So, we can actually use the $F$-test for this type of hypothesis testing because $F_{1,n-k-1} \sim t_{n-k-1}^2$.

```{webr-r}
#--- OLS ---#
reg_sc <- feols(lwage ~ jc + univ + exper, data = twoyear) # OLS

#--- F-test ---#
F_test <- car::linearHypothesis(reg_sc, c("jc-univ=0"))

#--- t-statistic ---#
sqrt(F_test$Chisq[2])
```

<br>

Check with the previous slide of the same t-test and confirm that the t-statistics we got there and here are the same.


:::
<!--end of panel-->

## Everything in this lecture is one idea

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The recipe

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Everything in this lecture was one recipe, and this is it, unchanged from the first slide. State the hypotheses. Find the distribution of a statistic assuming the null. Compute it. Pick a level, which fixes a critical value. Compare. Read the sentence at the bottom, because it is the useful compression: the only thing that varied from test to test was which statistic you built and which distribution you looked it up in. If a future test looks unfamiliar, ask those two questions and it usually stops being unfamiliar.

</details>

Every test we did followed the same five steps from the very first slide:

+ write down $H_0$ and $H_1$
+ find the distribution of a test statistic <span style = "color: red;"> assuming $H_0$ is true </span>
+ compute the statistic from your data
+ pick a significance level, which fixes a critical value
+ reject if your statistic is more extreme than that critical value

<br>

The only thing that changed from test to test was <span style = "color: blue;"> which statistic </span> you build and <span style = "color: blue;"> which distribution </span> you look it up in.

### The four tests

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

The four things we did, side by side. Read down the statistic column and notice how similar the first two are: an estimate, minus its value under the null, over its standard error. The only difference is what counts as the estimate. The third is genuinely different, because it compares two model fits rather than standardising a single number, and that is why it can answer a question the first two cannot. And read the two bullets: the covariance term is why the variance-covariance matrix had to appear at all.

</details>

| Question | Statistic | Distribution under $H_0$ | In R |
|---|---|---|---|
| Is one coefficient equal to a value? | $\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_j - \beta_j^0}{\widehat{se(\widehat{\beta}_j)}}$ | $t_{n-k-1}$ | `broom::tidy()`, or by hand |
| Is a linear combination equal to a value? | $\dfrac{\widehat{\alpha} - \alpha^0}{\widehat{se(\widehat{\alpha})}}$ | $t_{n-k-1}$ | `car::linearHypothesis()` |
| Are $q$ coefficients <span style = "color: red;"> jointly </span> zero? | $\dfrac{(SSR_r-SSR_u)/q}{SSR_u/(n-k-1)}$ | $F_{q,\,n-k-1}$ | `car::linearHypothesis()` |
| What range of values is consistent with the data? | the CI, not a test | $t_{n-k-1}$ | `broom::tidy(conf.int = TRUE)` |

+ the second row needs $Cov(\widehat{\beta}_1,\widehat{\beta}_2)$, which is why the variance-covariance matrix appeared
+ the third row is the only one that cannot be built from a single coefficient and its standard error

### How they relate

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Two connections that reduce the count. First, the F-test with one restriction is the t-test squared, which we confirmed numerically two slides ago. Second, and this one is worth internalising: a confidence interval and a two-sided test are the same statement. The ninety-five percent interval is precisely the set of null values you would fail to reject at five percent. So reporting an interval reports infinitely many tests at once, which is a good reason to prefer it. Then read the callout, which is the thing I most want you to carry away.

</details>

Two connections worth remembering, because they mean there are fewer ideas here than there appear to be:

+ **$F$ with one restriction is just $t$ squared.** $F_{1,\,n-k-1} \sim t_{n-k-1}^2$, which is why `car::linearHypothesis()` gave the same answer as the t-test we did by hand.

+ **The confidence interval and the two-sided test are the same statement.** The 95% CI is exactly the set of null values you would <span style = "color: blue;"> fail </span> to reject at the 5% level. If a CI excludes zero, the t-test rejects $\beta_j = 0$; if it contains zero, it does not.

<br>

:::{.callout-important title="The one thing to carry into your own work"}
An individually insignificant coefficient is <span style = "color: red;"> not </span> evidence of no effect. The MLB players and the simulation both showed variables that looked useless one at a time and mattered a great deal together. When variables are correlated, test them <span style = "color: blue;">jointly</span>.
:::

:::
<!--end of panel-->
